cases.cutoff: 2011, after a bacterial RNA-guided nuclease system and two required RNA components are known, before the 2012 programmable single-guide cleavage result

packet.pressure: A bacterial antiviral locus stores variable target-related sequences and uses a nuclease plus two RNA components. The system cleaves invading nucleic acid, but the minimal programmable mechanism and its transferability are unresolved.
availableEvidence: Genetic evidence indicates the locus participates in adaptive microbial immunity.
A large nuclease protein is required for one subtype.
A small trans-acting RNA and a target-derived guide RNA both participate in nuclease maturation/function.
Sequence complementarity appears central to target recognition.
Existing engineered nucleases can edit genomes but require protein engineering for each new target.
liveRoutes: continue descriptive microbial-immunity studies without engineering the nuclease
reconstitute the nuclease plus both RNAs in vitro and vary target/guide sequences
fuse or simplify the two RNA components into one engineered guide and test whether changing its target-matching segment redirects cleavage
move directly into mammalian cells before reconstructing the minimal cleavage mechanism
continue zinc-finger/TALEN-like protein-engineered nuclease development as the main programmable route
constraints: biochemical specificity must be demonstrated before broad transfer claims
the nuclease may require additional bacterial factors not represented in the current packet
sequence-specific cleavage is not equivalent to safe genome editing
off-target and cellular repair outcomes are unresolved

cases.hiddenOutcome: Biochemical reconstruction showed dual-RNA-guided sequence-specific Cas9 cleavage; an engineered single guide RNA made targeting programmable, followed rapidly by genome editing in eukaryotic cells.

cases.cutoff: late 2003, after large commodity clusters and a fault-tolerant distributed filesystem are described, before the MapReduce publication

packet.pressure: A web-scale operator repeatedly runs large scans, indexing, aggregation and transformation jobs over data distributed across thousands of commodity machines. Individual application teams keep rebuilding partitioning, scheduling and failure logic.
availableEvidence: Large clusters of inexpensive machines can deliver high throughput if software handles frequent component failure.
A distributed filesystem optimized for large files, append-heavy workloads and application-controlled replication/locality is in production.
Many data jobs naturally apply a local transformation to records and then aggregate/group intermediate values.
Programmers currently manage machine assignment, data movement, retries and stragglers explicitly.
Relational database systems provide higher-level data processing but do not directly match all current web-scale batch workloads or cluster assumptions.
liveRoutes: keep writing application-specific distributed job code
build a general batch scheduler but leave partitioning/data movement to applications
define a deliberately restricted map/partition then group/reduce programming model and let a runtime own partitioning, scheduling, locality and retries
move all workloads into a conventional parallel relational database
build reusable libraries for failure recovery and data movement without constraining the application programming model
constraints: programmers should still express custom computation
the runtime overhead must repay itself across many jobs
the abstraction cannot assume every workload fits perfectly

cases.hiddenOutcome: MapReduce exposed map/reduce functions while the runtime handled partitioning, scheduling, data movement and failures; the abstraction diffused through Hadoop and later required broader resource-management boundaries such as YARN.

cases.cutoff: 2010, after programmable GPUs and ImageNet are available, before the 2012 AlexNet result

packet.pressure: Visual recognition systems remain far from human-level robustness. Hand-engineered features plus conventional classifiers dominate strong benchmarks, while deeper neural networks are expensive and difficult to train at image scale.
availableEvidence: Backpropagation and convolutional neural networks are established techniques but have mixed large-scale performance histories.
Programmable GPUs expose very high parallel numerical throughput for non-graphics computation.
A new labeled image dataset contains millions of examples across roughly one thousand object classes and supports a large public recognition benchmark.
Unsupervised/deep pretraining has renewed interest in deeper representations.
Compute, memory, optimization and overfitting remain major constraints.
liveRoutes: continue improving hand-engineered visual descriptors and strong conventional classifiers
train a substantially larger convolutional network on the large labeled dataset using GPU acceleration and regularization
focus on unsupervised pretraining before any supervised large-scale model
distribute a much larger neural network across many machines immediately
reduce dataset/model size to keep experiments inexpensive and iterate on architecture first
constraints: evaluation must use held-out benchmark data
training must finish within practical experiment time
model capacity must not be judged only by training error
a benchmark win would not prove broad visual or semantic generality

cases.hiddenOutcome: A deep convolutional network trained on GPUs over ImageNet achieved a large held-out error reduction in 2012 and accelerated broad adoption of deep representation learning.

cases.cutoff: 2005, after inhibitory immune receptors and early CTLA-4 clinical translation are known, before PD-1 phase-I development and later multi-tumor response evidence

packet.pressure: Many cancer immunotherapies produce weak or inconsistent benefit. Animal evidence suggests tumors may exploit inhibitory immune checkpoints, but removing immune brakes can also cause severe autoimmunity.
availableEvidence: One inhibitory T-cell receptor has strong animal evidence that antibody blockade can enhance anti-tumor immunity.
Another inhibitory receptor/pathway has been characterized and is implicated in peripheral immune tolerance/exhaustion.
Monoclonal antibody manufacturing and early human oncology trials are feasible.
Prior immune stimulation/vaccine approaches have frequently disappointed.
Tumor shrinkage, survival, durability and immune toxicity can diverge.
liveRoutes: continue tumor-specific vaccines and cytokine stimulation as the main strategy
push the first checkpoint-blocking antibody through controlled clinical trials with explicit immune-toxicity management
develop blockade against the second inhibitory receptor/pathway and test it independently
combine multiple checkpoint blocks immediately before each has an interpretable single-agent evidence base
abandon systemic immune activation because autoimmune toxicity makes the mechanism unusable
constraints: serious immune adverse events are plausible
early tumor shrinkage is not sufficient evidence of durable benefit
different tumor types may respond differently
clinical development requires independent safety/efficacy evaluation and regulatory admission

cases.hiddenOutcome: Checkpoint blockade against CTLA-4 and later PD-1/PD-L1 produced durable clinical responses in subsets of patients across multiple cancers while retaining serious immune-related toxicity as a separate outcome axis.
